paragraphs: Hierarchical optimization involves decisions whose objectives depend on other decisions. The paper studies two structured versions: minimax problems with a nonconvex outer objective and a strongly concave inner problem, and bilevel problems with a nonconvex outer objective and a strongly convex inner problem. Its central concern is how to optimize them when gradient estimates contain noise of unknown magnitude.

The proposed algorithms combine momentum normalization with adaptive parameter choices. Their gradient-norm convergence rate has two terms: 1/√T and √σ̄/T^(1/4), up to logarithmic factors, where T counts iterations and σ̄ bounds gradient noise. The algorithms obtain this rate without receiving the noise level beforehand, allowing their behavior to adapt across low-noise and high-noise settings.

The contribution is a sharp convergence guarantee under the stated hierarchical problem structure, alongside experiments on synthetic and deep learning tasks supporting effectiveness. The gradient-norm guarantee concerns progress toward stationarity. Its practical significance is that achieving the stated noise-dependent rate does not require first knowing how noisy the gradients are.
neurips-2025-adaptive-algorithms-with-sh.tldr: Adaptive hierarchical optimization algorithms achieve sharp noise-dependent convergence guarantees without prior knowledge of gradient noise.

paragraphs: Diffusion models produce outputs through a refinement process, but many methods for spending additional computation at inference follow a fixed denoising schedule. Such schedules offer limited flexibility when individual inputs differ in difficulty or tasks call for different amounts of work. This paper frames adapting that computational effort during inference as a problem in its own right.

The proposed framework, Adaptive Bi-directional Cyclic Diffusion, treats inference as a search process. It refines candidate outputs through bidirectional diffusion cycles and adjusts both exploration depth and when to stop. Its three components organize this process around cyclic search, automatic balancing of exploration and exploitation, and adaptive thinking time. Together, they make the amount and direction of refinement adjustable.

Experiments report improved performance across diverse tasks while retaining computational efficiency. The stated finding supports using adaptive search to manage inference effort, rather than tying that effort entirely to a preset schedule. The contribution is therefore both a formulation of adaptive inference-time scaling and a framework that implements it through controlled diffusion cycles.
neurips-2025-adaptive-inference-time-sca.tldr: ABCD adaptively controls diffusion search depth and stopping to improve outputs while maintaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: CLIP can match images and text effectively while still struggling to understand how concepts relate within a scene or sentence. The paper highlights a distinction between sensitivity to wording and understanding meaning. According to the abstract, earlier compositionality improvements often favored the former, and their gains could come alongside worse image–text retrieval performance.

CLIC addresses this through a fine-tuning technique that combines multiple images with their associated captions. The method targets compositional understanding while retaining retrieval as an important outcome. Its reported improvements cover both lexical and semantic understanding across different architectures and differently pretrained CLIP models, suggesting that the training technique is useful across the tested starting points.

The experiments also report consistent retrieval gains, including for CLIPS, which already has strong retrieval performance. Short CLIC fine-tuning produces the best compositional CLIP model on SugarCrepe++ in the reported comparison. These findings matter because they connect better understanding of concept relationships with better retrieval, resolving the tension observed in the previous approaches discussed by the paper.
neurips-2025-advancing-compositional-awa.tldr: CLIC fine-tunes CLIP using combinations of images and captions, improving compositional understanding and retrieval together.

paragraphs: The paper asks what formal conditions could protect generative-model users against copying copyrighted training material. It revisits near access-freeness, a previously proposed sufficient condition, and shows that this condition alone does not prevent infringement. In particular, models satisfying it can still enable verbatim copying, which the authors describe as a tainted model.

To develop more meaningful guarantees, the authors introduce a blameless copy protection framework and a specific version called clean-room copy protection. This version relates a user's copying risk to their behavior in a hypothetical clean-room setting. A user can control that risk by behaving in a way that would be unlikely to produce copying in that counterfactual setting.

The paper also establishes a conditional connection to differential privacy: it implies clean-room copy protection when the dataset meets the authors' golden requirement for copyright deduplication. That dataset condition is essential to the stated result. The contribution replaces an insufficient guarantee with a framework that explicitly accounts for user behavior and the conditions under which privacy can provide copying protection.
neurips-2025-blameless-users-in-a-clean-.tldr: The paper exposes a flaw in an earlier copyright-protection condition and develops a clean-room guarantee that differential privacy satisfies under a deduplication requirement.

paragraphs: Cancer survival models often process whole-slide pathology images as many small patches because the original images are so large. This can be expensive and fail to preserve the slide's overall spatial organization. The paper focuses on relationships among components of the tumor microenvironment, whose spatial interactions are associated with prognosis.

ZTSurv works with slides downsampled by a factor of 50. Using tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte maps, it performs zero-shot segmentation of tumor and stroma, reducing the annotation effort needed from pathologists. It then extracts visual and semantic information from the different components and builds a heterogeneous graph. This graph represents their spatial intersections for predicting clinical outcomes within an end-to-end framework.

Evaluation across four cancer cohorts from TCGA reports better prediction results and substantially lower computational costs than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the usefulness of low-resolution tissue organization for this prediction task. The approach matters because it connects efficient component segmentation with explicit spatial modeling, addressing both annotation demands and the cost of processing whole slides.
neurips-2025-cancer-survival-analysis-vi.tldr: ZTSurv uses low-resolution tissue segmentation and spatial graphs to improve reported cancer survival predictions while reducing computation.

paragraphs: An image description can mention its main subject while leaving much of the scene unexplained. COCONut-PanCap addresses this lack of detailed coverage in image–text datasets by pairing fine-grained descriptions with explicit image regions. It builds on COCO images and COCONut panoptic masks to connect language with the areas of an image that language describes.

The dataset contains dense, human-edited descriptions grounded in segmentation masks. This grounding gives each region-level caption a corresponding visual area, supporting consistency between the text and the scene. The resulting annotations are intended for both vision-language models that interpret images and generative models that create images from text, making detailed regional correspondence useful in both directions.

The reported experiments show significant improvements across understanding and generation tasks, with benefits that complement large-scale datasets. COCONut-PanCap also provides a benchmark for evaluating panoptic segmentation and grounded captioning jointly. Its contribution is a form of annotation that brings scene coverage, region boundaries, and descriptive language together in one resource for training and evaluation.
neurips-2025-coconut-pancap-joint-panopt.tldr: COCONut-PanCap links detailed human-edited captions to segmentation regions, improving reported image understanding and generation performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to keep publishing statistical summaries of an incoming data stream while preserving differential privacy. The quantities of interest are its first and second moments, which underpin summaries such as means and covariance matrices. Joint Moment Estimation, or JME, estimates these quantities together with less noise than naive approaches.

The central idea is to analyze their privacy sensitivity jointly. This analysis identifies a particular privacy regime in which including the second-moment estimate has no additional privacy cost. The qualification matters: the result applies within that regime, and does not say second moments are always free to release. JME also supports the matrix mechanism, connecting the joint analysis to that estimation framework.

The authors demonstrate the method in running mean and covariance estimation for Gaussian density estimation, and in model training with DP-Adam. These applications show why coordinating the two estimates matters: both require information captured by first and second moments. The stated contribution is improved estimation accuracy through a shared privacy analysis while maintaining the required privacy protection.
neurips-2025-continual-release-moment-es.tldr: JME jointly estimates streaming first and second moments, identifying a privacy regime where second moments incur no additional privacy cost.

paragraphs: Urban reconstruction with Gaussian Splatting often uses LiDAR to supply geometric guidance. Obtaining accurately aligned LiDAR and camera data can be difficult because sensors differ in capture time and mounting position. D²GS develops a LiDAR-free reconstruction framework that instead builds dense geometric guidance from predicted depth.

The method first projects metric depth predictions from multiple views into a dense point cloud, then progressively prunes it to improve global consistency. Next, a Depth Enhancer uses diffusion priors from a depth foundation model to improve depth maps rendered by the Gaussians. Those enhanced maps feed back into Gaussian training as stronger geometric constraints. Additional constraints on Gaussian shape and normals target road geometry.

Experiments on Waymo report consistently better results than state-of-the-art comparisons, including more accurate geometry than methods using ground-truth LiDAR. The authors also report that their geometric priors are denser and more accurate while being as effective as LiDAR guidance. The contribution is a mutually reinforcing refinement process that improves predicted depth and reconstructed geometry together without requiring LiDAR input.
neurips-2025-d-2-gs-dense-depth-regulari.tldr: D²GS reconstructs urban scenes without LiDAR by jointly refining Gaussian geometry and dense predicted depth.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Group Relative Policy Optimization under binary rewards and identifies a question-difficulty bias arising from its group-relative advantage calculation. It also connects this reinforcement learning objective to discriminative supervised learning. These observations motivate DisCO, which trains reasoning models by raising the scores of positive answers and lowering those of negative answers.

DisCO replaces the group-relative objective with a scoring-based discriminative objective. It uses reinforcement learning scoring functions without clipping and directly handles a KL-divergence constraint through constrained optimization. The authors state that these choices eliminate the identified difficulty bias and address entropy instability, enabling long, stable training. The framework also accommodates discriminative techniques for situations where generated negative answers greatly outnumber positive ones.

Experiments improve mathematical reasoning in models already fine-tuned with supervision. Across six benchmark tasks, the 1.5-billion-parameter model gains an average of 7% over GRPO and 6% over DAPO. The findings support the paper's proposed connection between objective design, training stability, and reasoning performance in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2025-disco-reinforcing-large-rea.tldr: DisCO replaces group-relative training with constrained discriminative learning to remove identified difficulty bias and improve mathematical reasoning.

paragraphs: Discovering a symbolic partial differential equation from measurements requires finding both an equation's structure and its numerical coefficients. The search becomes difficult as spatial dimension increases, while measurement noise makes candidate expressions harder to evaluate accurately. ABL-PDE addresses these two challenges by combining logical knowledge with a neural learning module.

Its first-order logic knowledge base represents a variety of PDEs while constraining the candidate search space. The authors state that this restriction preserves expressive power and allows problem-specific knowledge to be incorporated. A consistency optimization process then links the knowledge base and the neural network, so symbolic reasoning and learning interact during equation discovery.

The paper reports robust identification of equation structure, accurate coefficient estimation, and improved stability as hyperparameters vary. Experiments on three benchmarks at different noise levels support the approach's effectiveness. The significance is that symbolic knowledge contributes directly to organizing the search, while the neural component participates in the same optimization process, addressing both the size of the hypothesis space and noisy evaluation.
neurips-2025-discovering-symbolic-partia.tldr: ABL-PDE combines logical constraints and neural learning to discover symbolic PDE structures and coefficients from noisy data.

paragraphs: Standard transformer attention has a quadratic time cost that limits scalability. Yet transformers also have established theoretical capabilities: they can simulate algorithms in the Massively Parallel Computation framework. This paper asks whether a faster attention mechanism can retain those capabilities, making efficiency and expressive power part of the same analysis.

The proposed Approximate Nearest Neighbor Attention, or ANNA, has subquadratic time complexity. The authors prove that transformers using ANNA preserve the previously established ability to match MPC algorithms. They also show that ANNA-transformers can solve the reasoning tasks Match2 and k-hop with near-optimal depth. These are guarantees about computational representation and required layers within the analyzed framework.

A further result shows that constant-depth ANNA-transformers can simulate constant-depth low-rank transformers. This makes MPC a shared language for comparing different efficient attention approximations. The paper's significance is therefore twofold: it introduces an efficient attention mechanism with expressivity guarantees and provides a unified theoretical approach for understanding how several forms of attention relate.
neurips-2025-fast-attention-mechanisms-a.tldr: ANNA provides subquadratic attention while provably preserving established transformer capabilities in a parallel-computation framework.

paragraphs: Robust partially observable Markov decision processes model an agent that sees only part of its environment and must tolerate uncertain dynamics. The paper describes this as a game: the agent chooses actions, while an adversarial nature chooses dynamics. Evaluating a fixed agent policy requires finding a sufficiently challenging nature policy, which is computationally difficult.

The authors first examine benchmark difficulty. Some problems can be solved by considering only restricted subsets of nature policies, potentially making them easier than their formulation suggests. They formalize this notion and construct three benchmarks requiring expressive nature policies. They also introduce an evaluation method based on solving an equivalent MDP and extend two POMDP upper bounds to the robust setting.

Those upper bounds efficiently approximate a policy's optimality gap and provide evaluation baselines. Experiments find that naive nature policies cannot solve the proposed benchmarks, that the evaluation method is accurate, and that the bounds offer solid baselines. Together, these contributions strengthen both the tests used for robust policies and the tools for assessing their quality.
neurips-2025-on-evaluating-policies-for-.tldr: The paper improves robust POMDP evaluation with demanding benchmarks, an equivalent-MDP method, and useful policy-quality bounds.

paragraphs: Long videos overwhelm vision-language models when each frame requires many tokens. Limited context then forces sparse frame sampling, losing temporal information. XComp addresses this by compressing both the representation of individual frames and the set of frames retained for a particular question.

Its token-level component, LP-Comp, trains progressive compression modules within language-model layers, targeting one token per frame at the final layer. This enables processing two to four times as many frames with improved performance. Its frame-level component, QC-Comp, uses internal attention scores to select question-relevant frames. To reduce attention's bias toward the beginning and end of long sequences, it splits videos into short segments and applies local attention.

XComp combines these mechanisms to support denser sampling with a larger compression ratio. Fine-tuning VideoChat-Flash with supervised compression tuning uses only 2.5% of the supervised fine-tuning data and raises LVBench accuracy from 42.9% to 46.2%, alongside gains on other long-video benchmarks. The results support learning compression jointly with question-sensitive frame selection as a way to retain useful information under context constraints.
neurips-2025-one-token-per-highly-select.tldr: XComp combines learned token compression and question-guided frame selection to fit more video information into limited context.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes requiring frontier AI laboratories to release small, openly accessible analog models. These would be scaled-down models trained similarly to, and distilled from, their largest proprietary systems. The proposal responds to concerns that safety regulation can impose costs that discourage innovation.

The authors argue that accessible analogs would let a broader research community investigate safety, interpretability, and algorithmic transparency. Researchers could work directly with these public proxies while laboratories retain their full-scale models. The argument draws on research described in the abstract showing that safety and interpretability methods developed on smaller models can generalize effectively to frontier-scale systems.

The paper presents reduced regulatory burden and faster safety progress as expected benefits of this policy. It also argues that reusing data and infrastructure would keep additional costs low. These are claims supporting a proposed mandate. The broader position is that expanding fundamental research access can deepen understanding of models and ease the tradeoff between safety and innovation, allowing progress on both objectives.
neurips-2025-position-require-frontier-a.tldr: This position paper argues that mandatory small analog models could broaden safety research while promoting innovation.

paragraphs: Reasoning Gym is a library of environments for training and evaluating reasoning models with verifiable rewards. It includes more than 100 tasks across areas such as arithmetic, algebra, geometry, graph theory, logic, cognition, computation, and games. This breadth provides multiple kinds of reasoning problems within a shared resource.

Its defining feature is procedural generation: environments can produce a practically unlimited supply of examples with adjustable complexity. Instead of being restricted to a fixed collection of questions, training and evaluation can use different difficulty levels and task configurations. The same underlying task can therefore support ongoing assessment as the conditions of the problems change.

The authors report experimental evidence that Reasoning Gym is effective for both evaluation and reinforcement learning of reasoning models. Its contribution is the combination of verifiable tasks, broad domain coverage, and controllable example generation. That combination makes the dataset's size and difficulty adjustable parts of the workflow, supporting continued training and evaluation across a range of reasoning demands.
neurips-2025-reasoning-gym-reasoning-env.tldr: Reasoning Gym provides over 100 procedurally generated reasoning tasks with adjustable difficulty for training and evaluation.

paragraphs: The asymmetric traveling salesman problem requires finding a low-cost tour when travel costs can depend on direction. This paper approaches the discrete optimization problem through a continuous relaxation, allowing gradient-based updates over soft permutations. The aim is to make tour construction amenable to differentiable optimization while retaining constraints that guide it toward valid solutions.

The framework combines a trace-based differentiable directed-acyclic-graph constraint with a doubly stochastic relaxation of assignment matrices. It optimizes these soft assignments using projected exponentiated gradients with an adaptive step size. After continuous optimization, a greedy post-processing procedure repairs subtours by merging cycles in a cost-aware way, producing discrete tours from the relaxed representation.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on standard asymmetric TSP benchmarks and competitive accuracy and scalability. They particularly highlight large or asymmetric instances where LKH-3 struggles. The contribution brings together differentiable structural guidance and explicit discrete repair: the relaxation enables gradient-based search, while the merging procedure handles the remaining task of recovering a complete tour.
neurips-2025-solving-the-asymmetric-trav.tldr: The method solves asymmetric tour problems through differentiable soft assignments followed by cost-aware subtour merging.

paragraphs: Diffusion planners trained on offline trajectories depend heavily on the quality and diversity of those trajectories. Limited data can restrict their ability to handle unfamiliar tasks or longer planning horizons. SCoTS addresses this through reward-free data augmentation, constructing extended trajectories by incrementally joining shorter segments.

The method first learns a latent representation that preserves temporal distances, capturing how states relate through time in the environment. It then stitches segments iteratively, guided by directional exploration and novelty. These guides encourage the constructed trajectories to cover and expand the represented state space, producing both longer sequences and a more diverse training collection.

On offline goal-conditioned benchmarks that require stitching and long-horizon reasoning, the authors report significant gains in diffusion-planner performance and generalization. The augmented trajectories also improve widely used offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning algorithms across diverse environments. This broader result supports the value of the generated training data beyond diffusion planning itself: organizing existing segments around temporal structure can make them more useful for learning extended behavior.
neurips-2025-state-covering-trajectory-s.tldr: SCoTS creates diverse, extended trajectories without rewards, improving reported long-horizon planning and offline goal-conditioned learning.

paragraphs: Recognizing a fine-grained video action requires relating the overall activity to its smaller component actions. Global descriptions alone can misalign videos and text because different activities share visual appearances or atomic actions. Some relevant actions are also brief or gradual, making them difficult to capture in a single overall video representation.

SFAR uses a storyboarding-inspired approach to describe actions at multiple levels. A language model generates descriptions of common atomic actions for each global semantic description. A filtering metric checks their correspondence with that global meaning without requiring video input for this description-refinement stage. The method then uses both levels of description to identify prominent frames and aggregate video embeddings more accurately.

Experiments across several action-recognition datasets report competitive performance in supervised, few-shot, and zero-shot settings. The stated contribution is a better connection between broad activity descriptions, their component actions, and the frames used to represent a video. This helps the matching process account for subtle actions that can be obscured by an exclusively global view.
neurips-2025-storyboard-guided-alignment.tldr: SFAR uses filtered atomic-action descriptions to select informative frames and improve fine-grained video–text alignment.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards needs problems with precise, checkable answers. Simply generating more questions can be inefficient when those questions do not address what a model needs to learn. SwS makes problem synthesis responsive to the model's observed weaknesses during reasoning training.

The framework defines weaknesses as questions the model repeatedly fails to learn through iterative sampling during reinforcement learning. It extracts the core concepts from those persistent failures and generates additional problems focused on them. Subsequent augmented training then targets these weak areas. This creates a feedback process in which training behavior determines what new material is synthesized.

The authors report average performance gains of 10% for 7-billion-parameter models and 7.7% for 32-billion-parameter models across eight reasoning benchmarks, without external knowledge distillation. These results support using a model's own failure history to guide data augmentation. The approach matters because it treats the usefulness of a new question as dependent on the learner's current capabilities, connecting problem generation directly to training needs.
neurips-2025-sws-self-aware-weakness-dri.tldr: SwS generates new reasoning problems from persistent training failures to target model weaknesses without external distillation.

paragraphs: Conventional point tracking loses its usual image-coordinate target when a point moves outside the camera's view. TAPVid-360 introduces a task that asks for the three-dimensional direction toward a queried scene point throughout a video, including when the point is far outside the observed narrow field of view.

The authors obtain supervision from panoramic videos. They resample these videos into narrow-view perspectives while tracking points across the full panorama with a two-dimensional pipeline to compute reference directions. This supports learning representations of the surrounding scene without requiring dynamic four-dimensional ground-truth scene models. The resulting TAP360-10k dataset contains 10,000 perspective videos with directional tracking annotations.

A baseline adapts CoTracker v3 to update directions through per-point rotation predictions. It outperforms the compared TAP and TAP-Vid 3D methods. The contribution combines a new task, a practical supervision source, and an initial model: together they make persistent awareness of off-screen points an explicit target for training and evaluation, extending tracking beyond the currently visible image.
neurips-2025-tapvid-360-tracking-any-poi.tldr: TAPVid-360 introduces directional point tracking beyond the camera view, supported by panoramic-video supervision and a 10,000-video benchmark.

paragraphs: The Common Pile addresses whether openly licensed text can support capable language-model pretraining at substantial scale. Earlier collection efforts, according to the paper, had been limited by size or quality. The authors collect and curate eight terabytes of text from 30 sources covering research, code, books, encyclopedias, educational materials, transcripts, and other domains.

They test the collection by training two models with seven billion parameters each. Comma v0.1-1T uses one trillion training tokens, while Comma v0.1-2T uses two trillion. This makes model training a direct validation of the dataset's usefulness, connecting the collection effort to the performance of models actually trained on its contents.

Both models achieve competitive performance against models trained on unlicensed text with similar computational budgets, including Llama 1 and 2 7B. The release includes the dataset, creation code, training mixture, and model checkpoints. These results support openly licensed pretraining as a practical direction at the evaluated scale, while the released materials expose both the underlying collection and its use in training.
neurips-2025-the-common-pile-v0-1-an-8tb.tldr: The Common Pile releases eight terabytes of openly licensed text and validates it with two competitively performing 7B language models.

paragraphs: Predicting brain responses to natural images often involves mapping neural-network features to measured brain activity. The paper argues that conventional linear mappings overlook the spatial and feature structure of those representations. Alternatives with fixed spatial receptive fields are also poorly suited to the dynamic routing involved in high-level visual processing.

The authors use transformer attention to route features organized by visual location toward category-selective brain areas. Because the routing depends on the input image, the model can represent changing relationships between image content and high-level regions. The attention signals can also be visualized, making it possible to inspect how different images direct information toward different categorical areas.

The method predicts brain activity during natural-scene viewing significantly better than the compared alternatives across feature models and measurement modalities. Its performance on novel images motivates the authors to propose it as a candidate mechanistic account of visual routing. That is a proposal supported by predictive and interpretability results, rather than a claim that the brain's routing mechanism has been definitively established.
neurips-2025-transformer-brain-encoders-.tldr: Attention-based brain encoders improve visual-response prediction and offer an interpretable candidate model of content-dependent visual routing.

paragraphs: Uni-Instruct develops a common theoretical framework for more than ten approaches to distilling diffusion models into one-step generators. The framework is based on a diffusion expansion theory for the f-divergence family. Its goal is both to explain existing methods through shared principles and to derive effective training objectives.

The expanded divergence is initially intractable to optimize directly. The authors introduce theoretical results that yield an equivalent tractable loss, allowing one-step models to minimize that divergence family. This links the unification to an implementable training method, so the theoretical account also produces a concrete route to improved generation.

Reported FID scores are 1.46 for unconditional and 1.38 for conditional CIFAR10 generation. On ImageNet at 64-by-64 resolution, the one-step model scores 1.06 versus 2.35 for its 79-step teacher. The paper also applies the method to text-to-3D generation, reporting slight improvements over SDS and VSD in quality and diversity. The findings combine strong image-generation results with a more modest extension to another generation task.
neurips-2025-uni-instruct-one-step-diffu.tldr: Uni-Instruct unifies diffusion distillation methods and derives a tractable objective yielding strong one-step generation results.

paragraphs: VideoMAR generates video from an image using a decoder-only autoregressive model with continuous tokens. It combines frame-by-frame temporal generation with masked spatial generation. The guiding design is that time should be causal, while positions within a frame can use information bidirectionally. A next-frame diffusion loss connects these two forms of generation.

To manage the difficulty of long sequences, training progresses from shorter to longer temporal spans and from lower to higher spatial resolutions. A progressive temperature strategy during inference mitigates accumulating errors. The model also combines temporal key–value caching with parallel spatial generation for efficiency, while three-dimensional rotary embeddings support extrapolation in space and time.

On VBench-I2V, VideoMAR outperforms Cosmos I2V while using 9.3% as many parameters, 0.5% as much training data, and 0.2% as many GPU resources in the reported comparison. These findings support combining temporal autoregression with spatial masked generation. The training curriculum and inference strategy address the practical difficulty of sustaining this generation process across a video.
neurips-2025-videomar-autoregressive-vid.tldr: VideoMAR combines temporal autoregression and spatial masked generation to achieve strong image-to-video results with substantially fewer reported resources.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation becomes more demanding when relevant information is visual. The paper identifies two problems: models may receive images without allocating enough reasoning to visual perception, and their search queries may fail to express what information they need. VRAG-RL trains vision-language models to handle these decisions through reinforcement learning.

Models interact with search engines and generate single-turn or multi-turn reasoning trajectories using visual perception tokens. Their action space includes cropping and scaling, allowing inspection to proceed from broad context to finer detail. A reward combines query rewriting and retrieval performance with a model-based reward, connecting search quality to the optimization of the reasoning process.

Across diverse challenging benchmarks, the authors report improvements over existing methods of 20% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 30% for Qwen2.5-VL-3B. These findings support training retrieval, visual inspection, and reasoning as interacting behaviors. The approach matters because successful answers depend both on finding relevant material and on examining its visual content at an appropriate level of detail.
neurips-2025-vrag-rl-empower-vision-perc.tldr: VRAG-RL trains vision-language models to improve visual retrieval and reasoning through adaptive search, cropping, and scaling.
